transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

I'm here because my mood has been incredibly unstable. For over a year, I felt unusually high-energy and elevated, but for the past six months, I've crashed into a deep depression and feel completely exhausted. I really need help managing these extreme shifts.
During the period when you felt high-energy and elevated, did you experience times where you were so restless or impulsive that it caused problems at work or in relationships?

Yes, I was incredibly restless and felt like I constantly had to keep moving or doing something. I couldn't tolerate just sitting still and would start multiple projects at once because of all that overflowing energy. It definitely caused some tension at work because I was trying to do too many things at the same time.
During those high-energy periods, did you ever experience any thoughts or perceptions that others found strange, like hearing voices or believing things that weren't true?

No, I never experienced anything like that. Even when my energy was really high, I didn't hear voices or believe things that weren't true. I always felt grounded in reality, just incredibly sped up and restless.
How many days in a row did you need to feel that high-energy, elevated mood before it started affecting your sleep or activities?

I definitely experienced those periods of elevated mood and high energy, but I'm not really sure exactly how many days in a row they would last before things started being affected. I just can't recall the specific number of days because everything felt like such a blur back then.
Can you recall if those high-energy periods lasted for at least four consecutive days, or were they shorter than that?
Oh, it was definitely much longer than just four days. That state of high energy and hyperactivity actually lasted continuously for about a year and two months.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Bipolar I Disorder", "Bipolar II Disorder"], but based on this conversation, Bipolar II Disorder seems unlikely because the patient reported a manic episode lasting over four days—specifically, a continuous high-energy state for about a year and two months—which meets the duration criterion for a manic episode. Bipolar I Disorder requires at least one manic episode, while Bipolar II Disorder involves only hypomanic episodes (which do not cause marked impairment or last at least one week). The patient's episode caused significant impairment at work and lasted far beyond four days, ruling out hypomania. Additionally, the absence of psychotic features means we do not need to consider Bipolar I with Psychotic Features as a separate diagnosis at this time. Therefore, the current candidate is solely Bipolar I Disorder.
